The Weight of Unsent Messages

I have a folder on my phone. It's called "Drafts" but it's really a graveyard. Forty-seven messages I never sent. Some are apologies that arrived too late. Some are confessions that would have changed everything, or nothing, or I'll never know which. One is just the word "hey" typed and deleted and retyped seventeen times before I closed the app and went to make tea instead.

We don't talk about this, do we? The architecture of almost-communication. The way we build elaborate structures in our minds—entire conversations, arguments, reconciliations—that never leave the skull. The other person lives in there too, a version of them we've written, responding to lines we've rehearsed. Sometimes they say exactly what we hoped. Sometimes they don't. We never find out because we never press send.

I think about the message I wrote to my grandmother three days before she died. I was going to send it after work. I was tired. I thought there would be time. There's always time, we tell ourselves, until there isn't. The draft is still there. "Grandma, I'm thinking about you. The garden looks good this year." Simple. Stupid. True. I read it sometimes like a prayer, like a curse, like evidence in a case I'm building against myself.

My therapist says I have trouble with completion. She's not wrong. I leave books half-finished, meals half-eaten, relationships half-ended. There's something comforting about the in-between, the potential. A sent message is a closed door. A draft is a door that could open onto anything. The imagination is generous. Reality is a specific room with specific furniture, and sometimes the furniture is uncomfortable, or missing, or arranged by someone else entirely.

But I'm tired of doors that don't open.

Last week I sent something I'd been drafting for months. A message to someone I loved, telling them I loved them, telling them I was afraid, telling them I didn't know what came next. I pressed send with my eyes closed. The phone felt hot in my hand. I waited. The typing indicator appeared, disappeared, appeared again. Finally: "I know. Me too."

We're still figuring it out. It's messy. There are silences that feel like failures and silences that feel like peace, and I'm learning to tell the difference. But I sent it. I let the door open. The room was different than I'd imagined—better in some ways, harder in others—but it was real. It was *happening*.

I deleted the other forty-six drafts that night. Not because they didn't matter, but because they were finished now, in their way. They had done their work, which was to keep me company in the dark, to prove I was capable of feeling, of wanting, of reaching. They were practice. They were proof of life.

Now I try to send things before I'm ready. Not everything—some things need to marinate, need to be tested against time and distance and the person I'm becoming. But the important things. The things that will change shape if I hold them too long, that will calcify into resentment or nostalgia or nothing at all. The "hey" that becomes a wall. The apology that becomes a grudge. The love that becomes a memory of love.

My grandmother would have liked the garden message. She would have called me, probably, because she never trusted text for anything important. She would have wanted to hear my voice, to know I was really there, really *me*. I think about this when I'm tempting to type instead of call, to draft instead of speak. Some things need the body. The breath. The risk of being heard in real time, with no edit button, no backspace, no folder called Drafts where we can hide our bravest selves.

I'm learning to be brave in real time. It's terrifying. Yesterday I told a friend I was struggling, really told them, didn't soften it, didn't make it funny. They cried. I cried. We sat in my kitchen and didn't fix anything. It was the best conversation I've had in months.

The folder is empty now. I check it sometimes, out of habit, expecting to find something there. But I'm trying to live in the sent. In the said. In the done, even when it's done badly, even when it's done too late, even when the response is silence or anger or a door closing that I can't reopen.

Especially then.

The drafts were beautiful. They were safe. They were mine alone. But I want to be known. I want to be *reachable*. I want the mess of actual connection, with all its failures and repairs, its misunderstandings and clarifications, its "I didn't mean it that way" and "I did" and "let's try again."

I'm trying again. Every day. The tea is cold now. I should go make another cup, or better, go find someone to drink it with. Someone to talk to. Someone to listen. Someone to let in.

The door is open. I'm walking through.
